From the st. Louis Globe Democrat.


Globe Democrat reporter few days ago wit
messed "horse dentist" engaged at his very pecu-
liar and interesting work at Arnot's stable. DR..
Clark was the operator, and several valuable trot-
ting horses, the private property of well-knOwn
gentlemen, where the patients. From travelling
bag he took dozen gttering steel implements.
There were in the lot giant forceps, pattened like
those used by ordinary dentists. Peculiarly shaped
instruments they were, modelled for special emer-
gencies and particular teeth. There peculiar
rasps Of graded coarseness, which were applied
to long steel handles. Delicate and coarse saws,
cruellooking cutting forceps, steel tooth and
brushes-in fact, an entire outfit of the usual i'm
plements of the dentist, only greatly enlarged
scale.


The first animal brought forth was a beautiful
mare belonging to Mr.. Garneau. She seemed
nervous and fretfId. One side of her mouth was
cut as by the bit. The animal had formed habit
of throwing her head to one side, and the lacera-
tion of the mouth was caused by the driver pull
ing the head around to proper position.


DR.. Clark took the halter from her head, laid
his hand upon her nose looking steadily into her
eyes, and then run hand back into the cavernOus
mouth, and felt around for moment. When his
hand reappeared, he said, "There are excrescenees
and ragged growths upon the outside of the grind
ers. These lacerate the mucous membrane, and





The Doctor then adjusted one of the small fine
rasps to its handle, and it away back into the
mouth, and began working it rapidly, but regular
ly. harsh, grating filing noise was heard, which
set the cold chis chasing each other down the re-
porter's spinal column and caused his teeth to
stand on edge The horse took the matter much
more calmly, standing perfectly still, and to all
appearances, enjoying the operation. Rasps or
files of finer face were used and when the last
was applied but little sound given out. The
other side of the mouth was treated in the same
way, and then, with new style Of implement the
Doctor turned his attention to the incisOrs and
''canine teeth" in the front of the mouth. Their
edges were rough and uneven. More filling, with
some rough and delicate scraping, and the DOct'
then ceased his labors and invited the company to
look at the result. He opened the mares lips, and
her teeth stood revealed and white as ivory, with
edges straight and perfect, all rough edges gone
and even the tarter removed. The teeth looked
as regular and perfect those of a human being.
The mare "whinnied" her appreciation of the i'm
provement in her mouth as she was led away.


The next horse was known as "poor feeder"
and was constantly troubled with collie and indi-
gestion. The animal sobbered in unpleasant
way. brief examination showed that the ex-
cresences were on both sides of the mOlars, and
the tongue and mucous membrane were so acera-
ted and irritated that the mastcation of foot was
painful to it, and in consequence it ate as little
possible, and that imperfectly. The dentist went
to work and in half an hour had all the teeth in
that horses head as smooth and pleasant to the
touch as a billiard ball. "Take care now, that he
don't eat up the stable" said the Doctor, as boy
led the horse away.


Several cases of this kind were treated, and then
a "cribber" was brought out "Cribbers" are also
called "stump- suckers" They continually gnaw
hitching- posts trees, feed-racks anything that
they can get their teeth on. The animal does it
to relieve a numb unpleasant sensation caused by
the crowdng of the front teeth. The colored man
who led this also sufferer out said: 'Look out,
boss he is an eater, you bet. / guess he could
gnaw telegraph pole in about five minutes, if
you'd leave i'm" The Doctor at once saw what
was the matter and produced fine saw. In two
seconds narrow slit was cut between the teeth,
and thoroughly eased, the animal remanded
to his STALL


The cruel-looking fOrceps with sharp edges in
brief order disposed of the superhuous growth of
what would be called a snag tooth. The animal
WINGED a little, but the Doctor, without any coax
ing or petting held him still, and the job was soon
over.


The last patient of the day was young horse
with the to0thache The gum was liberated about
the roots of the moar, and the animal was in great
pain. The halter was taken off, the horse was
quieted and the tooth carefully examined. The
Doctor selected pair of forceps to suit the case
and then, with q rapid movement and a powerful
wrench pulled out the tooth before the horse even
suspected his design. He danced around quite
lively for a very brief space, came again under
control of the Doctor, who fixed up the gum in
good shape and then was led away happier
horse.

proyements have been made in the spectrcscope

and the scientists are accordingly eager to test
their powers on the outer envelopes of the sun,
which are only visible during the period OF to-

appendages the secret of their composition.

tricts, and to judge from the present indications

the one over the lakes The high pressure con-
tnucs on the Middle Atlantic and New England
coast, but it is rcccding into the ocean gradu-
ally. The pressure is relatively high, but fall
ing over the South Atlantic and Gulf districts.
Rain has fallen only in the northern lake regions.
the Missouri Valley and on the Middle Atlantic
coast. Cloudy weather prevails in all the dis
tricts except the southern portion of the central
valley districts and the South Atlantic and Gulf
roasts. A general rise in temperatures has taken
place, except In the Northwest, where they have
been variable. The winds are from fresh TO

and the Middle Atlantic and New England

probable that when the depression that is now
IN the West shall have moved to the lower lake
regions the gradients will become very stcep.
particularly over the New England and the
northern section Of the Middle Atlantic coast
districts, so that brisk winds may be expected in

able that the two depressons may consolidate

General Crock, General Ingalls,, General Ludington

garding Indian affairs. From information received

all captured returned. Apprehension still
exists in many quarters of renewed troubles
in Oregon and Washington this coming spring.
and some Indians are reported being discontcnted
regarding their reservations. When asked his opinion

for the coming year is not improved. He had
cautioned stockmen and settlers some years ago to

men it was stated on good authority openly pur-

sweep the stockmen and settlers of Central and
Northern Nebraska from the face Of the earth. the
Sioux were formerly rich in ponies but their num-
bers are now much reduced year ago renegade
whites stole 200 from them and the Sioux. who
visit the responsibility for such acts the
ment. called on Crook for an explanation. and said

tinue and efforts to stop them while encouraged by

taking steps toward breaking up a variety of Sun
day trespassing which prevails in the neighbor-
hood of Willow Grove and other shores in that
locality. The trespassers are generally young
men and boys from the city who 60 down to these
shores in sailboats and skifs, build fires upon the

henrOosts and nests have been robbed, their barns

woods, jeopardizing property of value. In one
instance a barn was burned down in this way.

The thermometer yesterday in New York
indicated an exceptionally high tempera-
ture, the highest experienced here this year.
The memories of former heated terms were
revived by the signs Of suffering presented
on all sides, by the painting pedestrians and
the exhausted street car and stage horses.
The temperature having mounted toward
the nineties by an almost imperceptible
gradation during the past week people did
not realize that the summer heat was upon
them SO soon after the cool and almost chill
ing breezes of the previous days. But yes
terday the rays of Old Sol shot downward
with an intensity that rendered prolonged
exertion almost impossible. Toward night,
however, cloudiness, the natural result Of
this great atmospheric heat and the attend
ant evaporation, overcast the heavens
and the Saint rumbling of distant thunder
indicated that Nature was adjusting her
thermal balance by that peculiar process
that compensates while it temporarily dis
turbs. Advices from London inform us
that the heat in that city has become very
great. Only few days ago we published
accounts from the West Indies of oppressive
temperatures. Recent volcanic disturbances
in the western and South American regions
have doubtless charged the atmosphere
with an undue amount of heat, and this,
with the seasonable addition from the solar
source, has been moving over the Northern
and Southern hemispheres from west to
east with the volumes of atmosphere affected
by it. Our special meteorological reports
from the Atlantic show that the tempera-
ture has been steadily increasing from west
to east during the past eight or ten days.
In the West and Southwest the weather has
been very warm, but temporary change to
cooler airs may be looked for within day
or two.

On last Thursday Chas. Nash was

Nash had been fishing in the creek

stopped to ascertain, and at that
moment the snake struck him, the
fangs entering his right heel and
holding the reptile fast to the foot
while the young man moved off
quite distance, only releasing
him when the flesh gave way. The
bitten man at once proceeded to the
hotel, where he drank large guam
tity of whisky, thus doubtless saw
ing his life. He was then brought
to San Jose, where medical attend :
ance was obtained and efficient
remedies employed; and though the
entire leg became perfectly black
and fearfully swollen, science con-
quered, and he is now convalescent.

WIxFoID, Ireland. June 2. 1878.
The steamer Idaho, Captain Holmes. of
the Guion line, struck on the Carrigmore
rocks, of Saltee Islands, last night, during
heavy fog, and foundered soon after No
lives were lost, oil the passengers and crew
being sent ashore in the steamers boats.


A DENSE roc.


The Idaho sailed from New York on May
81 and arrived at Queenstown at ten min
utes to one Saturday afternoon, where she
landed the mails and several passengers.
She then proceeded on her way to Liver
pool. During the evening dense fog rose
Georges Channel, sounding the fog whistle
and using the utmost precaution.


THE ROCK STRUCK.


The fog was SO dense that the position of
the Carrigmore lightship could not be ac-
curately fixed, and at ten minutes past one
o'clock the Idaho struck the rock and began
to take in water. Captain Holmes instantly
ordered the boats launched. The discipline
was good, and the boats were found in sea-
worthy condition.


SAVING THE LADIES.


The frst to enter tho boats was Mrs.
Norman and her little son, Hubert Norman,
this lady having no gentleman escort. The
first officer stood Mt the gangway and had
the six other ladies passed into the boat,
after which the husbands Of ladies already
there were allowed to join them. This
boat. containing the ladies and children,
was the first to leave the ships side.


COURAGE OF CAPTAIN HOLMES.
Captain Holmes was the last person to
leave the ship-his boat was only about
thirty yards from tho vessel when she dis
appeared. The Idaho went down within
twenty-five minutes after she struck. Tho
passengers speak very highly Of Captain
Holmes conduct. lie was on the bridge,
with the first officer and the pilot, when
the ship struck Had it not been for his
GOODNESS and presence Of mind some lives
would certainly have been lost.


ArLoAr IN THE Foo.


After rowing for about four hours the six
boats made Saltee Island and all tho passen-
gers and crew were landed in safety. There
being only ono house on the island very
little accommodation could be provided for
tho passengers. The carc-taker who resides
there Immediately gave up his house to the
ladies.


ARRIVAL AT WEXFORD.


The passengers were oil landed on the
mainland this morning and conveyed to
Wexford, where they were taken care of by
Mr.. J. W. Walsh. Lloyd's agent here. All
aro in good spirits. and very thankful for
their preservation.


BAGGAGE ALL LOST


Owing to the fact that tho disaster oc-
Cured in the middle OF the night. and that
after reaching the deck the vessel was found
to be in a sinking condition, not a particle
Of clothing was saved, and the passengers
brought away with them only such valu-
ables as they had upon their persons.


TnE vas Eel DISAPPEARS.


The Idaho Is found to have disappeared
completely, having sunk in nineteen fa-
thoms of water. The passengers arc to be
conveyed TO Liverpool by way Of tho Dub
lin, Wicklow and Wexford Railway to Dab
lin, and thence by steamer.

of last week gets off the following rather improb

Recently gentleman who resided two or three
miles from the city employed tramp of unusu-

satisfaction that day after day the job con-
tinued The employer wanted to give him place

thought it would be giving too much trouble and
walked into the city every night, but was at work
bright and early in the morning. The employer
fed and offered to pay cash wages nightly but the
tramp declined taking it until the whole job was
done, and then was willing to receive less than
the wages ordinarily paid, but to this the gentle
man would not assent and the tramp taking his
money they parted the best of friends. Such
case is worthy of mention, for it shows how wick
ed and unjust the prejudice against ragged and
hungry tramps may be. The gentleman is one
who recently held prominent official position"

This case was given to the jury yesterday,
and they are still out. In the number Of
recent murder cases few have received more
continued attention than this and it has
been the fortune Of this trial to fall in
period when the papers are literally
crowded with criminal chronicles and in
quries of the most intense interest But
neither the Silver Lake inquiry, nor the
Stannard case, nor the strange develop
ments of the Bridgeport slaughters, nor
dozen other current narratives scarcely
away from the semi-savage domestic
drama unfolded in the story Of the North
cumberland murder. Husbands and wives
at war are, unfortunately, not unfamiliar
figures to the reader who gives any atten-
ton to the court reports but this husband
and this wife were apparently at war with
vigor and viciousness not common, and,
while the husband did not appear to adver-
tise the domestic dissensions, the wife
fairly carried them into the street, made
them noisy and coarse scandals, talked of
them in terms which it is generally un-
derstood decent people do not use, and
filed the mind of an only daughter
with that fierce feminine hate against her
father which the mother herself apparently
felt. AS soon as this woman was slain sus-
picion was directed against the husband,
and the general assumption that he had a
motive for so great crime was an uncon-
scious evidence of the opinion entertained
of the wife's acts. No other conceivable
person was known to have any motive what
ever, and this common thought has kept
interest alive through many phases of the
case. With the evidence tor the prosecu-
tion put in it was generally believed
that Billings was dead man but when
the evidence for the defence came it was
conceded that the facts sworn to established
a clear alibi. In his address the counsel
for the prosecution has somewhat revived
the first impression against the prisoner,
and has shaken the dependence upon the
alibi; yet it remains the great feature and
hold of the Defence and stands upon the
straightforward evidence of some sincere
witnesses. The cloud raised as to the mis-
sile with which the murder was done has
been also all in favor of the prisoner, and
in virtue of these two great points there is
fair ground for doubt Of the prisoners
guilt, and this doubt might we'll vitiate a
clearer case than that made out for the
prosecution. There seems very little like
lihood, therefore, that the verdict will be
that the prisoner is guilty, but there may
be disagreement.

What night for moonlight rambcs the lovers

In Anthony Trollope's "Barcheste


Tower" there is an ecclesiastical gath


ering pictured-a reception given b,


the new bishop of an English diocese


IN which the hostess, ''Mrs. Proudie


moved about with well-regulated grace


measuring out the quantity of her ia


vors according to the quality of hel


guests. ;"


1t is amusing to see how many "Mrs.


Proudies" there are in Washington.


And it is-not-amusing to see how


many nice little wives and good. plain


mothers soiled by taste of gayety in


our republican capital. One members S


wife, when she came here first, few


months ago, was really home-sick for her


little village. But after the cards came


in to her, and she began to fully realize
that she was the wife of a member of
Congress, what airs the country mite
took on herself! Ladies whose claim to
distinction rested upon their innate re-
hnement and intelligence, and not upon
theaccidental position of their husbands.
were passed unnoticed save by the faint
est smilinssless inclination; and the egrade.
or GOODNESS with which the wife of the
new member welcomed them. The
change in the toilet of the lady was mark
ed. Her eye eagerly ran over the dress
es of her acquaintance. From a modest
lady in a plain black silk and smooth
brown locks she burst into the less dis
hneue style of light satin and bare shoul-
ders, and pyramid-shaped head with the
surrounding thatch of frizzes which hides
the broad, beautiful brow. The lady
now trips to her hired cab every day,
and gives her orders to the coachman
with anicy, fault finding tone which she,
poor soul, does not know indicates her
newness to the luxury of a hired team
and livery. Her days are round of
careless, meaningless toadyism; her
nights wild revels, where neither sense
nor comfort ever show their plain, old
fashioned faces.


This woman, before her husbands
election, would have sat up with her
neighbor's sick child. She would have
made its tiny grave clothes and put
flowers in its dead hands, the while her
eyes were misty with sympathy. With
her own needle and thread she would
have put the Grape bands on the parents
and watched that no jarring
sound or care grated upon them the lit
tie while they were left alone with their
dead. She would have stayed in the
and put away little dresses
and broken toys while the family were
at the cemetery. She will never do it
again. Never again find time for the
sweet amenities of life, or the comfort
ing sympathy with the bereaved. She
will never again be satisfied to live in a
country town, or 60 to church sewing
societies, or sit up with the sick. She
is above that now. And yet she was
sweet young girl; a fair young wife; a
gentle young mother.


Left in retirement she would have
bloomed out long, fragrant life of good
deeds, and been truly mourned at her
death. Sore hearts that she had bound
up would have remembered her, per-
haps, as a clear-eyed saint, who wore
soft white cap and plain alpaca dress
in her old age, and on autumn Sundays,
when quiet hung like benediction over
the still woods, they would have led
little children around the simple head
stone, have loitered and told of her
lovely life until the memory breathed
into infant hearts would, like the seed
in the soft mellow earth, have brought
forth good deeds in some future strait.
Thus, although dead, she would live
again. But now she is spoiled for
everything. She will fly her round,
fritter away her day, drop out of life,
and not ripple on the tide of fashiona-
Bile society will show where she has gone
down. She will perchance have big
but her eulogy will be mean
ingless, and her epitaph awaken no ten
der thought in any heart.


There are hundreds of women, the
currents of whose lives have been turned
by the veering winds and treacherous
sand bars along this coast. Power makes
fools of men admiration makes fools of
women. They can't stand it. They have
not independence to set up and carry
on an ideal life which would satisfy their
thirsting minds and elevate their souls.
They are not bad, nor really weak, but
they drift into the sameneSs and mean
ingless round, and in time the whirl be-
comes second nature, and they cannot
strike out a straight line for themselves.

The golden-rods and weeds of May,

Charles Ogesby. colored laborer at the Louisville

sweetheart Kate Strauss goodlooking mulatto girl,
Sunday night For the past two years Kate and
Charles have been living together in unlawful COM

Deep interest Is taken here to-day in the narrative

MADE A SLAVE 10 THE CHIEF.

menial Offices. She allowed to meet talk

riors several times left the party and returned with

olic and educated at Jesuit college. He told

from the Yankton agency. but were few from Red

borhood Of small village in Northern Nebraska.
where the Indians procured liquor and they all be-
came drunk That night Mrs. Jones escaped, having
on only ragged blanket and one moccasin. She
travelled south being guided in her course by the
stars, and subsisting for many days on raw arti-
chokes. After five six days she met occasional
emigrant wagons moving northward. and Mrs. Jones
was given dress. She begged her way through the
State reaching her old home in Iowa the last day of
